title: Paper Coffee Cups Release Millions of Nanoplastics
paragraphs: A takeout coffee might seem simple — it's a hot drink in a paper cup. But there's more going on inside that cup than you might think.
Although paper cups are mostly made of paper, they usually have a thin plastic lining to prevent liquid leaking through, and to help keep the cup strong.

Previous research has found that when plastic is exposed to higher temperatures, it generally releases more microplastics. And a new study from the University of Queensland in Australia wanted to know whether the type of plastic lining in these cups makes a difference too.

The researchers compared two types of plastic lining. One was polyethylene, or PE, which is made from fossil fuels. The other was polylactic acid, or PLA, which is a biodegradable alternative made from things like corn or sugarcane.

The researchers wanted to see how many nanoplastics each type of lining would release. Smaller than microplastics, nanoplastics are so small that even the largest are 70 times smaller than the width of a human hair.
When exposed to hot water, both linings released these tiny plastic particles — but unfortunately for fans of biodegradable plastics, the PLA lining released more.
The researchers found that PLA-lined cups released around 4.3 million nanoplastic particles per milliliter of hot liquid, compared with 2.7 million particles for PE-lined cups.

Elvis Okoffo, one of the study's authors, said the findings don't mean that PLA itself is unsafe, however. But he also pointed out that the implications of plastic particles on human health are still unclear.
"We know the chemicals in plastic aren't meant to be consumed," he said.
The study raises a bigger question about how food and drink packaging is assessed.
Okoffo said regulators should consider whether testing for microplastic and nanoplastic release should become part of safety assessments, especially for products used with hot liquids.

He also said consumers should be given information about the materials used to line their cups, while regulators could consider safety guidelines or product warnings. Manufacturers could also develop new linings that release fewer particles.
